title: About us
text:
Palaeoverse is a community-driven initiative advancing open science in palaeontology through shared tools, training, and resources.
Founded in 2022 by Lewis A. Jones, Palaeoverse grew out of a simple but widespread frustration: palaeontologists were independently reinventing the same workflows. Without standard tools or protocols for cleaning and preparing data, duplicated effort was the norm and reproducibility suffered. A group of early-career researchers decided to do something about it.
The result was the palaeoverse R package, a toolkit designed to streamline data preparation and exploration for palaeontological research. What began as a pragmatic solution to a shared problem has since grown into something larger: a formally organised initiative spanning a full software ecosystem, hands-on training workshops, community resources, and spaces for researchers at all career stages to connect and collaborate.



Members of the Palaeoverse team meeting in London in April 2026. From left to right: Lewis A. Jones, William Gearty, Joseph Flannery-Sutherland, Erin Dillon, Bethany Allen, Cecily Nicholl, Etienne Bacher.

title: Contribute to Palaeoverse
text:
Thanks for stopping by! Looking to find out how you can contribute to Palaeoverse? You have come to the right place!
We very much appreciate and encourage community contributions. Your contributions help shape and improve Palaeoverse packages to address community needs. Contributing is also a great way to build your coding and computational skills, share your expertise, and expand your research network. Contributions are recognized in a variety of ways, including in documentation files and on the Palaeoverse website, depending on the nature of the contribution.
If there is anything that is unclear within this guide, please let us know via Zulip, email, or by logging an issue so we can improve it.
There are multiple ways to contribute to Palaeoverse. This page will go through each of them, from engaging with the community to contributing code.

title: Contribute to Palaeoverse
text:
Sharing knowledge and resources
In addition to participating on Zulip, you can also share knowledge or resources by presenting in our monthly lecture series, or suggesting additions to our list of resources.
More generally, if you are interested in what we do, feel free to reach out at info@palaeoverse.org.
The remaining sections will focus on the software components of Palaeoverse. Engaging in these subsequent steps requires having a GitHub account (more information here).

title: Contribute to Palaeoverse
text:
Logging or discussing GitHub issues
Code-oriented tasks that need working on are logged as Github ‘issues’ within the respective Palaeoverse GitHub repositories (e.g. current rphylopic issues can be found at github.com/palaeoverse/rphylopic). If you find a bug in our code, or want to request a new function or feature, this is the best place to document it. Here you can also discuss outstanding issues, including helping us to prioritise tasks (even adding an emoji in support or protest to an issue is useful).

title: Contribute to Palaeoverse
text:
Contributing to code or documentation
If you want to get involved with contributing code or documentation to our packages (e.g. fix a bug or improve a vignette) but don’t know where to start, you can begin by browsing the outstanding issues. Once you find an issue that you want to address, we ask that you add a message in the issue to let people know that you are working on it.
If you are just getting started with collaborative coding, we recommend looking for issues labelled ‘Good First Issue’. These issues are relatively small and/or simple in scope, and are less of a time commitment than larger feature requests. Feel free to find an unclaimed ‘Good First Issue’ that interests you, ‘claim’ it by adding a comment to it, and jump in!
The section below presents an overview of the process to contribute code, but we also have a more detailed guide to explain the entire process, from installing required tools to submitting your changes in a pull request.

Contribution workflow (pull request process)
The contribution workflow below requires you to have basic knowledge of git and Github. If this is not the case, you can reach out to one of the core team members via email and they can make a pull request on your behalf, or help to guide you through the pull request and review process. However, you will be expected to respond to any reviewer comments on GitHub yourself (see below).
To make a pull request:

You (the contributor) should fork the repository (e.g. for the palaeoverse R package)

Clone the desired repository to your personal computer

Create a new git branch for your modifications (you should not make changes directly on the main branch)

Make your changes

Commit your changes (make sure your commit message is informative and concise)

Push your commits to your forked repository

When your changes are complete, you should submit them for merging via a pull request (“PR”) on GitHub

Note that a complete pull request should include a succinct description of what the code changes do, proper documentation (via roxygen2), and unit tests (via testthat). Only the description is required for the initial pull request and code review (see below), but pull requests will not be merged until they contain complete documentation and tests.
You also have to ensure that you follow our AI policy.


Minor changes
You can fix typos, spelling mistakes, or grammatical errors in function documentation and vignettes directly on GitHub (note that Github will automatically create a fork for you). However, note that fixing typos in the function documentation (those in the “Reference” page on the package website) requires editing the source in the corresponding .R file and then running devtools::document(). Do not manually edit an .Rd file in the man folder.


Substantial changes
If you would like to make a substantial change (e.g. add a new argument to an existing function or create a new function), you should first file an issue and make sure someone from the development team agrees that it’s needed (this prevents potentially wasted effort).
If you’ve found a bug, please file an issue that illustrates the bug with a reproducible example. The reprex package is very useful to build a minimal reproducible example.


The life of a pull request
Submitting a pull request for one of Palaeoverse’s R packages will automatically initiate several checks via GitHub Actions, such as R CMD check, linting and formatting checks, and test coverage check (among others). These checks will conduct some automatic review to ensure the new code doesn’t break any existing functionality and follows code standards.
Once these automated checks pass, at least two members of the Palaeoverse core team will manually review the changes before merging the pull request. This review should happen within a few days of opening a pull request. Note that if your pull request is not complete, it should be converted to draft.
Submitting a pull request is a big step, but it rarely happens that a pull request can be merged as-is. Like during the peer-review process for a journal article, reviewers will have questions and comments that you will need to address via the GitHub interface. If fixes and/or changes are required, you are expected to make these changes. Handling reviewers’ feedback might not be easy and can even feel adversarial sometimes, but remember that everyone has the same objective: producing good quality software. The Tidyteam code review guide is a great resource to understand better what is expected from you during code review and how reviewers will assess your code.

title: GitHub Actions
text:
View source file
So far, we have been running various checks (e.g. R CMD check) locally. This has two main drawbacks.
First, we may simply forget to run these checks, in which case we might discover bugs a long time after introducing them, making the debugging process more painful.
Second, our check results only apply to our development environment. We might run these checks in a new R session, but our results may depend on our R version, on other dependencies in our system, or on our operating system!
An essential tool in software development is continuous integration, often referred to as “CI”. The objective of CI is to run a battery of automated checks on every change in the repository, whether it be when we push a new commit to the main branch or when someone opens a pull request. In this section, we are going to explore some CI tools and workflows dedicated to R package development. Since GitHub is the most popular code hosting platform, we are going to focus on their own CI services, Github Actions, but the content of this section can be transposed to other platforms.

title: GitHub Actions
text:
GitHub Actions
GitHub Actions (sometimes abbreviated to “GHA”) is a service provided by GitHub to run CI workflows. We will demonstrate how to use it by adding a workflow to run R CMD check on every commit to main, on every commit to a PR, and on multiple operating systems and R versions.
Keep in mind that a CI workflow is not limited to checking R packages. It is essentially a list of steps where each step can run some code. Therefore, you can create workflows to check spelling in your repository, to run code stylers and linters, to check that all URLs are valid, and many other things.

A basic workflow for R CMD check
We will start by creating a new basic workflow for R CMD check. This will run on a single OS and only when we push a change to main. In practice, we rarely create workflows for R package development from scratch. Instead, we use a collection of workflows maintained on another GitHub repository: r-lib/actions. In particular, the examples folder contains many examples of useful workflows.
We will start by adapting the workflow named check-release.yml. For clarity, we will rename this file R-CMD-check.yaml. All GHA workflows need to be stored in the .github/workflows folder. Hence, we end up with the following file:


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

name: R-CMD-check

permissions: read-all

jobs:
  R-CMD-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      GITHUB_PAT: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      R_KEEP_PKG_SOURCE: yes
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          extra-packages: any::rcmdcheck
          needs: check

      - uses: r-lib/actions/check-r-package@v2
        with:
          upload-snapshots: true
          build_args: 'c("--no-manual","--compact-vignettes=gs+qpdf")'

There is a lot to unpack here! The on block tells GitHub when this workflow should be run. For now, we only want to run it when we push a new commit to main. We then have the name and permissions of the workflow. In some cases, we want to give some write access to workflows to make automated commits for instance, but here we can leave it as read-all.
The jobs part is where we define the steps that will be run by our workflow. Note that one workflow can run multiple jobs, but here we just have one named R-CMD-check. This will run on ubuntu-latest (the most popular Linux distribution). In most R-related workflows, we will find the next three steps: actions/checkout, r-lib/actions/setup-r, and r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies, that are here to install R and our package dependencies.
Once this is done, the last step is to run R CMD check via r-lib/actions/check-r-package.


Run this workflow in more cases
This is a good start but for now it only runs when we push changes to main. This is a bit too late, we would like to run this in a PR so that test failures due to changes in a PR do not affect the “clean” development version. We can tweak the on block to run this in pull requests as well:


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

[ ... ]

Now, this workflow will run on every change in every pull request.


Expanding R versions and platforms
We now run this more frequently, which addresses the first drawback of running tests locally (the developer might forget to run them), but it doesn’t fix the second drawback (depending too much on the developer environment). Let’s now run this workflow on more platforms and with more R versions!
To avoid adding one jobs per configuration option, we can create a matrix with all our desired inputs:


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

[ ... ]

jobs:
  R-CMD-check:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.config.os }}
    name: ${{ matrix.config.os }} 

    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        config:
          - {os: ubuntu-latest}
          - {os: macOS-latest}
          - {os: windows-latest}

[ ... ]

We have added a matrix of config options. For now, each config has a single key, os, that contains the operating system we want to use. We can retrieve this value with ${{ matrix.config.os }}, which we use both in runs-on (to actually change the OS used by the workflow) and in name (so that we can easily distinguish the output of these CI workflows).
We can add more keys to the config, such as an r key to define the R version we want to use.


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

[ ... ]

jobs:
  R-CMD-check:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.config.os }}
    name: ${{ matrix.config.os }} (${{ matrix.config.r }})

    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        config:
          - {os: ubuntu-latest,  r: 'release'}
          - {os: macOS-latest,   r: 'release'}
          - {os: windows-latest, r: 'release'}
          - {os: windows-latest, r: 'oldrel-1'}

[ ... ]

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: ${{ matrix.config.r }}

[ ... ]

We added r: 'release' to use the latest stable version of R, and r: 'oldrel-1' to use the previous R version. We use this matrix.config.r key in two places: in the name (for the same reason as before), and in the setup-r step, where we actually install R.
We still have a single workflow, but it now runs four different jobs with various OS and R versions. Note that you could also add more ancient R versions.


Some changes for a better developer experience
We could stop here, but instead I would like to highlight two changes that improve the efficiency and robustness of CI workflows.
The first one is about timeout. GitHub Actions is a very useful tool, but it depends on many external factors, starting from the fact that if GitHub has some issues then GHA might be affected. On top of that, issues in R versions or R dependencies can lead to longer-than-usual workflows that sometimes run for hours! Using the timeout-minutes parameter is an easy way to avoid this problem.


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

[ ... ]

jobs:
  R-CMD-check:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.config.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 20

[ ... ]

Using a 20-minute timeout is in general more than enough to check a standard R package.
The second change is to use concurrency. When we work in a pull request, we may push several commits in a few minutes, and each of these commits triggers the workflows. The default behaviour is to queue workflows, which can significantly slow us down since we have to wait for workflows associated to early commits while we are only interested in the results for our last commit.
The concurrency parameter changes this by automatically cancelling workflows if a newer one is triggered:


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

[ ... ]

name: R-CMD-check

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.head_ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:

[ ... ]



Final workflow
For reference, here is our final workflow:


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

name: R-CMD-check

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.head_ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions: read-all

jobs:
  R-CMD-check:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.config.os }}
    name: ${{ matrix.config.os }} (${{ matrix.config.r }})
    timeout-minutes: 20

    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        config:
          - {os: ubuntu-latest,  r: 'release'}
          - {os: macOS-latest,   r: 'release'}
          - {os: windows-latest, r: 'release'}
          - {os: windows-latest, r: 'oldrel-1'}

    env:
      GITHUB_PAT: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      R_KEEP_PKG_SOURCE: yes

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: ${{ matrix.config.r }}

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          extra-packages: any::rcmdcheck
          needs: check

      - uses: r-lib/actions/check-r-package@v2
        with:
          upload-snapshots: true
          build_args: 'c("--no-manual","--compact-vignettes=gs+qpdf")'

title: GitHub Actions
text:
GitHub Actions
GitHub Actions (sometimes abbreviated to “GHA”) is a service provided by GitHub to run CI workflows. We will demonstrate how to use it by adding a workflow to run R CMD check on every commit to main, on every commit to a PR, and on multiple operating systems and R versions.
Keep in mind that a CI workflow is not limited to checking R packages. It is essentially a list of steps where each step can run some code. Therefore, you can create workflows to check spelling in your repository, to run code stylers and linters, to check that all URLs are valid, and many other things.
A basic workflow for R CMD check
We will start by creating a new basic workflow for R CMD check. This will run on a single OS and only when we push a change to main. In practice, we rarely create workflows for R package development from scratch. Instead, we use a collection of workflows maintained on another GitHub repository: r-lib/actions. In particular, the examples folder contains many examples of useful workflows.
We will start by adapting the workflow named check-release.yml. For clarity, we will rename this file R-CMD-check.yaml. All GHA workflows need to be stored in the .github/workflows folder. Hence, we end up with the following file:


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

name: R-CMD-check

permissions: read-all

jobs:
  R-CMD-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      GITHUB_PAT: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      R_KEEP_PKG_SOURCE: yes
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          extra-packages: any::rcmdcheck
          needs: check

      - uses: r-lib/actions/check-r-package@v2
        with:
          upload-snapshots: true
          build_args: 'c("--no-manual","--compact-vignettes=gs+qpdf")'

There is a lot to unpack here! The on block tells GitHub when this workflow should be run. For now, we only want to run it when we push a new commit to main. We then have the name and permissions of the workflow. In some cases, we want to give some write access to workflows to make automated commits for instance, but here we can leave it as read-all.
The jobs part is where we define the steps that will be run by our workflow. Note that one workflow can run multiple jobs, but here we just have one named R-CMD-check. This will run on ubuntu-latest (the most popular Linux distribution). In most R-related workflows, we will find the next three steps: actions/checkout, r-lib/actions/setup-r, and r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies, that are here to install R and our package dependencies.
Once this is done, the last step is to run R CMD check via r-lib/actions/check-r-package.
Run this workflow in more cases
This is a good start but for now it only runs when we push changes to main. This is a bit too late, we would like to run this in a PR so that test failures due to changes in a PR do not affect the “clean” development version. We can tweak the on block to run this in pull requests as well:


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

[ ... ]

Now, this workflow will run on every change in every pull request.
Expanding R versions and platforms
We now run this more frequently, which addresses the first drawback of running tests locally (the developer might forget to run them), but it doesn’t fix the second drawback (depending too much on the developer environment). Let’s now run this workflow on more platforms and with more R versions!
To avoid adding one jobs per configuration option, we can create a matrix with all our desired inputs:


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

[ ... ]

jobs:
  R-CMD-check:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.config.os }}
    name: ${{ matrix.config.os }} 

    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        config:
          - {os: ubuntu-latest}
          - {os: macOS-latest}
          - {os: windows-latest}

[ ... ]

We have added a matrix of config options. For now, each config has a single key, os, that contains the operating system we want to use. We can retrieve this value with ${{ matrix.config.os }}, which we use both in runs-on (to actually change the OS used by the workflow) and in name (so that we can easily distinguish the output of these CI workflows).
We can add more keys to the config, such as an r key to define the R version we want to use.


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

[ ... ]

jobs:
  R-CMD-check:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.config.os }}
    name: ${{ matrix.config.os }} (${{ matrix.config.r }})

    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        config:
          - {os: ubuntu-latest,  r: 'release'}
          - {os: macOS-latest,   r: 'release'}
          - {os: windows-latest, r: 'release'}
          - {os: windows-latest, r: 'oldrel-1'}

[ ... ]

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: ${{ matrix.config.r }}

[ ... ]

We added r: 'release' to use the latest stable version of R, and r: 'oldrel-1' to use the previous R version. We use this matrix.config.r key in two places: in the name (for the same reason as before), and in the setup-r step, where we actually install R.
We still have a single workflow, but it now runs four different jobs with various OS and R versions. Note that you could also add more ancient R versions.
Some changes for a better developer experience
We could stop here, but instead I would like to highlight two changes that improve the efficiency and robustness of CI workflows.
The first one is about timeout. GitHub Actions is a very useful tool, but it depends on many external factors, starting from the fact that if GitHub has some issues then GHA might be affected. On top of that, issues in R versions or R dependencies can lead to longer-than-usual workflows that sometimes run for hours! Using the timeout-minutes parameter is an easy way to avoid this problem.


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

[ ... ]

jobs:
  R-CMD-check:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.config.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 20

[ ... ]

Using a 20-minute timeout is in general more than enough to check a standard R package.
The second change is to use concurrency. When we work in a pull request, we may push several commits in a few minutes, and each of these commits triggers the workflows. The default behaviour is to queue workflows, which can significantly slow us down since we have to wait for workflows associated to early commits while we are only interested in the results for our last commit.
The concurrency parameter changes this by automatically cancelling workflows if a newer one is triggered:


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

[ ... ]

name: R-CMD-check

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.head_ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:

[ ... ]

Final workflow
For reference, here is our final workflow:


.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

name: R-CMD-check

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.head_ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions: read-all

jobs:
  R-CMD-check:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.config.os }}
    name: ${{ matrix.config.os }} (${{ matrix.config.r }})
    timeout-minutes: 20

    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        config:
          - {os: ubuntu-latest,  r: 'release'}
          - {os: macOS-latest,   r: 'release'}
          - {os: windows-latest, r: 'release'}
          - {os: windows-latest, r: 'oldrel-1'}

    env:
      GITHUB_PAT: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      R_KEEP_PKG_SOURCE: yes

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: ${{ matrix.config.r }}

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          extra-packages: any::rcmdcheck
          needs: check

      - uses: r-lib/actions/check-r-package@v2
        with:
          upload-snapshots: true
          build_args: 'c("--no-manual","--compact-vignettes=gs+qpdf")'

title: Test a package
text:
View source file
We have a working package! We have checked that it can run locally and that results are as expected, so everything seems fine.
In practice though, a package will almost always evolve in some way: we may want to add new features, such as new function arguments or entire new functions, a user may report a bug that we need to fix, maybe we will want to add more documentation at some point, among other possible changes.
As we incorporate these changes, we need to make sure that we are not breaking other functionalities of the package. We could keep running some checks manually, but this quickly becomes tedious and error-prone, or we might just forget to do it.
An essential step in package development is to build a test suite that can run every time we change something. Building a test suite reassures:

title: Test a package
section: How to write a test suite?
text:
How to write a test suite?

Set up the test suite
There exist several packages to create and manage a test suite. The most famous one is testthat, but you might also be interested in tinytest.
To start using this package, run:


usethis::use_testthat()

✔ Setting active project to "/path/to/my.pkg".
✔ Adding testthat to Suggests field in DESCRIPTION.
✔ Adding "3" to Config/testthat/edition.
✔ Creating tests/testthat/.
✔ Writing tests/testthat.R.
☐ Call usethis::use_test() to initialize a basic test file and open it for editing.
This created a folder called tests:
my.pkg
├── DESCRIPTION
├── NAMESPACE
├── R
├── man
├── my.pkg.Rproj
└── tests
    ├── testthat
    └── testthat.R
We can now add tests files in tests/testthat. By convention, we name test files test-<name of the file to test>.R, such as test-n_unique.R.






Tip



If you have the R file you want to test opened in the editor, you can run usethis::use_test() to automatically create and open the corresponding test file.




Getting started with tests
When using testthat, a test is composed of a test_that() call that contains the title of the test and the code for the test, and one or several expect_*() calls that define your expectations, i.e. what the code should do.
Let’s see how we could test n_unique(). This function counts unique values in a vector, so it should work with any type of vector, e.g. numeric, character, logical, etc. We can start by writing some cases that are easy for us to check:


tests/testthat/test-n_unique.R

test_that("n_unique works with all types of vector", {
  expect_equal(
    n_unique(c(1, 2, 3, 1, 3)), # The function we want to test.
    3                           # Our expectation.
  )
  expect_equal(
    n_unique(c("a", "b", "c", "c", "c")),
    3
  )
})

We now want to check that our tests pass. There are a few ways to do that.
The simplest way is to simply evaluate the entire test_that() block defined above. We could also run the code inside test_that() line by line, but for now let’s evaluate the entire block at once. Note that we need to run devtools::load_all() first to ensure that we use the latest version of our functions and that testthat is loaded in the session:
test_that("n_unique works with all types of vector", {
  expect_equal(
    n_unique(c(1, 2, 3, 1, 3)), # The function we want to test.
    3 # Our expectation.
  )
  expect_equal(
    n_unique(c("a", "b", "c", "c", "c")),
    3
  )
})

Test passed with 2 successes 🥇.
Our tests pass! This approach is fine when we want to test one or two test_that() blocks, but it would quickly become annoying when we have more tests. We can use devtools::test() to run the entire test suite instead:
> devtools::test()
ℹ Testing my.pkg
✔ | F W  S  OK | Context
✔ |          2 | n_unique                                                                           

══ Results ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 2 ]






TipRun a subset of test files





It can quickly become annoying to run the entire test suite when we work on a single function. We can use the filter argument in devtools::test() to run a subset of all test files.
For example, devtools::test(filter = "unique") would only run test files whose name contains “unique”.



In both cases, our tests depend on the global environment, which is not ideal because test results might vary across sessions. Therefore, it is recommended to run tests in a clean R session. In RStudio, you can also use the “Test” button:



Being imaginative when writing tests
Testing the behaviour of our functions in reasonable use cases is an essential first step, and it already gives us a lot of confidence when we will modify the package in the future.
However, keep in mind that users will always find annoying interesting bugs in your software. When writing tests, it is important to think of all the ways your functions might be misused. In practice, we will never be able to catch all these cases, but trying to address as many as possible early on already leads to massive improvements in user experience! Spending a little bit of extra time on this when we create the test suite can save a lot of time in the future.
Let’s try to make sure our function covers corner cases!
For instance, we should make sure that missing values, NaN, and empty vectors are properly handled:

test_that("n_unique works with missing values", {
  expect_equal(n_unique(c(NA, 1)), 2)
})

test_that("n_unique works with NaN", {
  expect_equal(n_unique(c(NaN, 1)), 2)

  # NA and NaN are not the same thing
  expect_equal(n_unique(c(NaN, NA)), 2)
})

test_that("n_unique works with empty vectors", {
  expect_equal(n_unique(c()), 0)
})

and indeed these tests also pass:
> devtools::load_all()
ℹ Loading my.pkg
> devtools::test()
ℹ Testing my.pkg
✔ | F W  S  OK | Context
✔ |          6 | n_unique  

══ Results ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 6 ]






NoteWriting tests first?



In this module, we defined the function before starting on tests. An alternative approach to software development is called “test-driven development” (TDD). It stems from the idea that writing the function first gives an incentive to only write tests that will pass, because we don’t want to go back to modify the function in case we find something that goes wrong.
TDD reverses the order of development: we write tests first, laying out all our expectations about how the function should behave ideally, both in simple cases and in more complex cases. Only when this is done, we start writing and refining the function until it passes all of our expectations.


So far, we have only used expect_equal(), but there are many other functions to describe our expectations:

expect_length()
expect_type()
expect_named()
expect_warning()
and more…



Testing errors
Sometimes, throwing an error is the expected behaviour. For instance, n_unique() (without any input) should give an error because the function requires x, even if x itself is empty. One way to do this is to use expect_error():

test_that("n_unique errors if no input is provided", {
  expect_error(n_unique())
})

This helps, but it could be better because we don’t know the error message that users will actually see. We can improve this test by providing a regular expression that the error message should match:

test_that("n_unique errors if no input is provided", {
  expect_error(
    n_unique(),
    regexp = '"x" is missing'
  )
})

Still, this only ensures that our message matches this expression, but maybe some parts of the message are very confusing and do not help the user solving the problem.
The best way to test error messages is to use a snapshot test to capture the entirety of the user-visible output.






NoteA snapshot test?





Snapshot tests are tests that capture the output as users see it. They are very useful to check side effects of function calls, such as printing messages and warnings, or when the output appearance is key, e.g. for functions that produce plots.
We can define snapshot tests with expect_snapshot(). See this vignette on snapshot tests for more information.




test_that("n_unique errors if no input is provided", {
  expect_snapshot(n_unique(), error = TRUE)
})

Note that this expectation will only be checked when it is run non-interactively, meaning that copying this block and running it in the R console will simply skip the test. It has to be run via devtools::test() or via the “Test” button in RStudio.
> devtools::test()
ℹ Testing my.pkg
✔ | F W  S  OK | Context
✔ |   1      7 | n_unique                                                                                                       
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Warning (test-n_unique.R:28:3): n_unique errors if no input is provided
Adding new snapshot:
Code
  n_unique()
Condition
  Error in `n_unique()`:
  ! argument "x" is missing, with no default
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

══ Results ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[ FAIL 0 | WARN 1 | SKIP 0 | PASS 7 ]
On the first run, a warning says “Adding a new snapshot”. From now on, this test will always compare the output of n_unique() (with no input) to this error message. If the message changes in the future, then this test will fail and the snapshot will either need to be updated, or the change in the message will need to be reverted.


Click to see the entire test file for n_unique()



tests/testthat/test-n_unique.R

test_that("n_unique works with all types of vector", {
  expect_equal(
    n_unique(c(1, 2, 3, 1, 3)), # The function we want to test.
    3 # Our expectation.
  )
  expect_equal(
    n_unique(c("a", "b", "c", "c", "c")),
    3
  )
})

test_that("n_unique works with missing values", {
  expect_equal(n_unique(c(NA, 1)), 2)
})

test_that("n_unique works with NaN", {
  expect_equal(n_unique(c(NaN, 1)), 2)

  # NA and NaN are not the same thing
  expect_equal(n_unique(c(NaN, NA)), 2)
})

test_that("n_unique works with empty vectors", {
  expect_equal(n_unique(c()), 0)
})

test_that("n_unique errors if no input is provided", {
  expect_snapshot(n_unique(), error = TRUE)
})








CautionExercise



Your turn! Add some tests for safe_log().




Skipping tests
At some point, depending on the features of your package, you might want to skip some tests, and testthat provides a family of functions to handle these cases. For example, you could skip tests that:

depend on another package, using skip_if_not_installed()

test_that("...", {
  skip_if_not_installed("dplyr")
  ...
})

require an Internet connection (e.g if you’re building a package wrapping an API), using skip_if_offline()

test_that("...", {
  skip_if_offline()
  ...
})

cannot work on macOS, using skip_if_os()

test_that("...", {
  skip_if_os("mac")
  ...
})




Do we have enough tests?
We now have some tests in our package, but do they cover all function arguments? All possible use cases? We can use the package covr to see how much of our package is covered by tests:

covr::report()


Here, we only cover 20% of the package because safe_log() is still untested.






Caution



Code coverage gives information on which parts of the code are never tested, but it doesn’t mean that the covered parts are correctly tested!
For example, our n_unique() would get a 100% coverage with our first expect_equal(), which is by no means enough to ensure that this function works correctly.




More on tests
Testing software is not trivial and there is a lot of literature on this topic. We list below some other testing practices that may be worth exploring but won’t be covered in this module:

parametrised testing: a way to deduplicate tests by defining a lot of input combinations. See the R package patrick.
property-based testing: a testing framework where we define a property that the code should respect, and we test this property by generating many random inputs and checking whether this property is respected. An example of application is a package that implements a known method in a faster way (or with other features). Property-based testing can help ensuring that the old and new softwares give the same results. See the R package quickcheck and this blog post.
fuzzy testing: a testing framework where inputs are generated randomly. This encompasses property-based testing. See the R package CBTF.
mutation testing: a framework to complement test coverage. It helps ensuring that our tests actually check the function’s behaviour. It modifies small pieces of code in our functions, e.g. replacing > by <, and then runs the test suite. If these changes do not lead to any test failures, then it means that our test suite isn’t robust enough, even if the code coverage is high. See the R packages mutator and muttest.

Check a package
We have seen how to run tests, but we can now perform a more thorough check with devtools::check() (or the button “Check” next to “Test” in RStudio).
This is more comprehensive since it will perform a number of additional checks (on top of running the test suite), such as ensuring that you use all of your dependencies, that all examples in the documentation can run, and much more.

title: Mentorship Scheme
text:
What is the Mentorship Scheme?
Through the Palaeoverse Mentorship Scheme, you will upskill from software user to creator across six months of online learning, working alongside a cohort of early career researchers and under the mentorship of experienced Palaeoverse members. You will learn best practices for coding and package design in the R programming language as well as how to manage a software development project from start to finish. The scheme will culminate in code contributions to the Palaeoverse software ecosystem, and will deliver transferable data science skills that you can apply in your own research. There will also be opportunities to develop your own teaching skills at future in-person Palaeoverse workshops, hackathons and conference events.
By the scheme’s end, you will become a champion for open science, open-source tools, and reproducibility in palaeobiology. You will be able to implement robust data science workflows in R more efficiently, and will gain the skills to design and publish new software collaboratively to a professional standard. You will also be primed to convey these skills to your peers, setting you up for continued success in academic or industry settings.
Detailed information on the Palaeoverse Mentorship Scheme can be found below. If you have a question that is not addressed fully, or want to discuss your application with us, then please reach out on social media or via email info@palaeoverse.org. You can also join our community platform on Zulip and ask questions in the Community channel.

title: Mentorship Scheme
text:
Who is the scheme for?
The scheme is intended for early career researchers who currently use R in their work, and who wish to advance their coding ability and develop skills in collaborative software development and open science. We anticipate that it will be most beneficial to MSc/PhD students or recent doctoral graduates with a reasonable foundation in R, but who have little to no prior experience with GitHub workflows, package development, or contributing to open-source projects. The scheme is targeted towards software development for palaeobiology, therefore an undergraduate or master’s degree in palaeobiology or a related discipline (geology, evolutionary biology, etc.) will benefit your application.
The scheme is not intended as an introduction to R programming, nor will other programming languages be directly addressed. Applicants should be comfortable with most or all of the following:

importing and manipulating simple data in R
working with basic R data structures (e.g. vectors, data frames, lists)
writing and running their own scripts, or a script written by someone else
installing R packages and using their functions

We seek to widen the diversity of people involved in open science, especially in palaeobiology, via our mentee cohorts. We therefore actively encourage applications from underrepresented groups in the palaeobiology, open science, and software development communities.

title: Mentorship Scheme
text:
How does the scheme work?
The Palaeoverse Mentorship Scheme will be run online over six months. All content will be delivered in English using the digital platforms Github, Zoom and Zulip. Live sessions will take place at the start of each month, with the time zone to be decided based on the geographic composition of the cohort. As such, you will need a laptop with a webcam, mic, and a reliable internet connection. All other content can be completed asynchronously, at your own pace, allowing you to balance its completion with your other commitments. Scheme time is anticipated to occupy no more than 3–4 hours a week.
At the start of the scheme, you will be paired with a mentor from the Palaeoverse Team who will support your development towards championing open science and software engineering in palaeobiology. There will be a live seminar with the entire cohort in the first week of each month. Live sessions will be recorded in case you are unable to attend, although all mentees will be asked to prioritise live attendance where possible. In the other weeks, you will complete a self-guided or collaborative learning module, or work on code contributions to the Palaeoverse ecosystem of R packages, supported by mentor meetings in the first and third weeks. Mentor meetings will be organised at your mutual discretion to maintain flexibility.
The course will be structured as follows:

Months 1–2: Modules in scripting, function design and data science
Month 3: First code contribution
Months 4–5: Modules in advanced R package design and optional topics
Month 6: Second code contribution and presentation of the completed project

Please note that final content may be subject to change.
At the end of the scheme, you will receive a certificate of participation, endorsing your skillsets in code development, data science best practises, and open science principles.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
The ggplot2 basics

The most important function in the ggplot2 package is ggplot(). Note that this function doesn’t include the “2” of the package name. Let’s go ahead and try using this function on our penguins data.


ggplot(penguins)

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Theming

The last basic thing you might want to do with ggplot2 is modify the style of the visualization. This is extremely customizable, but the first place to start is with a built-in theme. I personally prefer the classic theme, which looks very similar to base R plots:


ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic()

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text: More complex features

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Other layers

There are many other types of plots that we can make with ggplot2.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Histograms

We can visualize the density of values for a single variable with a histogram:


ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, fill = species) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Boxplots and Violin Plotss

We can visualize the density of values for a single variable across a discrete variable with boxplots or violin plots:


ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
2D Contours

We can also visualize the density of values across two continuous variables using a 2D contour:


ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Time Series

Since there isn’t really any time series data in the penguins dataset, we’ll take a quick detour and use the built-in economics dataset to explore visualizing a time series. In this case, we are looking at unemployment over time:


ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Combining layers

We can also combine multiple layers to show the same data in different ways in the same plot. For example, we could show the raw data for the above contour plot in addition to the contours:


ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(30, 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12, 23)) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) + # don't expand the axes so the background is all filled
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Facetting

Let’s take our scatterplot example from earlier:


ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Saving plots

The last big thing you’ll need to know about plotting is how to save your plots. ggplot2 comes with a nifty ggsave() function which you can use to save your plots in a number of different formats. Here we’ll save our most recent combined plot as both a PDF and a JPEG. The former is a vector format, meaning all of the elements of the figure as geometric shapes, and, because of this, none of the data is lost (aka “lossless”). The latter is a raster format, meaning the figure is converted to a 2-D array of colored pixels of a desired size, and because of this, some of the data is lost in the process (aka “lossy”). This results in the pixellation that you see when you zoom in on a JPEG. ggsave() detects what format you want based on the file extension, so we just need to specify the file location and the object to be saved (and optionally the dimensions of the output file). It’s usually a good idea to keep all figures in their own folder (which was already created for you).


gg <- (g1 | g2) / g3
ggsave("figures/penguins_1.pdf", gg, height = 10, width = 10)
ggsave("figures/penguins_1.jpg", gg, height = 10, width = 10)

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
The ggplot2 basics
The most important function in the ggplot2 package is ggplot(). Note that this function doesn’t include the “2” of the package name. Let’s go ahead and try using this function on our penguins data.

ggplot(penguins)








You’ll notice that the ggplot() function doesn’t actually do much by itself. Here, we provide it with the penguins dataset, but the result looks like someone started making a plot and then stopped after the first step of making the rectangle for the plot area. This is because ggplot2 is designed around the “grammar of graphics”. Therefore, it expects you to build a sentence-like structure out of its functions. A single word (i.e., the call to ggplot() above) doesn’t make much of a sentence, so let’s start building up a real sentence.
By using the ggplot() function, we are essentially stating that we are beginning a plotting “sentence”. We then combine this with other “words” (function calls) using the + operator. The next component you usually want to specify in a ggplot “sentence” is our “aesthetic” mappings. These specify the columns of the dataset that correspond to each axis of the plot, including the x/y axes, but also the axes of color, shape, etc. We do this with the aes() function:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len)








Hey, it’s starting to look like a plot now! Except there isn’t any actual data being plotted. Let’s fix that. We’ll start off with a simple scatter plot by using the geom_point() function:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len) +
  geom_point()








And there we go! You’ll notice that with just a few lines, we’ve already made a pretty nice visualization of this penguin data. ggplot2 does most of the work for us once we specify our dataset and our x and y variables.






NoteMissing data



You may have noticed a warning that some rows of the dataset contain missing values. There are two penguins without any measurements in the dataset. How might we remove them using dplyr so we don’t get this warning over and over?






CautionSolution






penguins <- penguins |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(body_mass))






Now, let’s go a step further and color the points by another variable (e.g., the island of the penguins). With ggplot2, all that requires is specifying another aesthetic:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island) +
  geom_point()








Notice that ggplot2 comes with its own default color scheme. However, I would strongly discourage you from using the default colors, especially as the number of categories increases (with only 3 categories here it isn’t too bad). Let’s try out some of the more accessible color palettes that are also available in R.
First, let’s try one of the viridis color palettes. Since this palette is included in ggplot2, all we need to do is add the proper “scale” to our ggplot() call. Scales tell ggplot how to handle a particular aesthetic, and are usually of the form scale_[aesthetic]_[type]().

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) # avoid yellow at the end of the palette








Now let’s try one of the brewer color palettes.

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")








Outside of color, there are many other aspects of the graph that we can modify using aesthetics and “scale”s. For example, we can modify the shape of the points:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")














NoteMore missing data



Urgh, more missing data! It appears that nine of the penguins are missing sex identification data. We can ignore the warning message, but that extra “NA” category in the legend is quite annoying. We can remove this category from the legend using na.translate = FALSE within scale_shape_discrete() (you could also use scale_shape_manual() if you wanted to supply your own shapes):

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE)










And the x/y axes:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)")

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Theming
The last basic thing you might want to do with ggplot2 is modify the style of the visualization. This is extremely customizable, but the first place to start is with a built-in theme. I personally prefer the classic theme, which looks very similar to base R plots:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic()








Using this built-in theme has changed many visual aspects of the graph, including changing the plot background color, adding axis lines, and removing the internal grid lines. If you look very closely, however, the axis tick labels are still a slight grey. We can use the theme() function to further customize the appearance and change this. In this case, we’ll make the axis text elements have a black color instead of the default gray.

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








And there we have it! With just 10 lines we’ve created what I would say is a publication quality graph! ggplot does a lot of the tedious work for us, giving us time to focus on the more important aspects, such as labeling and color. Admittedly, I’ve spent a LOT of time on these aspects in the past…
More information about all of the hierarchical theme components that you can customize is available here. In order to change many of these components, you need to use theme elements like we did above with element_text(). That and other theme elements are documented here.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
More complex features

Other layers
There are many other types of plots that we can make with ggplot2.

Histograms
We can visualize the density of values for a single variable with a histogram:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, fill = species) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














Note



Histograms don’t require a y-axis aesthetic by default. The counts are tabulated for you. If you specify a “fill” aesthetic, the default is to stack the bars which can sometimes be a bit misleading. You can also dodge them to fix this:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, fill = species) +
  geom_histogram(position = "dodge") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))












Boxplots and Violin Plotss
We can visualize the density of values for a single variable across a discrete variable with boxplots or violin plots:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))









ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_violin(scale = "width", draw_quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














NoteGeom options



Note that many of these “geom”s have lots of options. For example, here we’ve decided to scale all of the violin plots to the same width and to draw the quartiles on them (mimicking the boxplots above). You can see all of the options for a geom by checking out it’s help page (?geom_violin) or on the ggplot website.




2D Contours
We can also visualize the density of values across two continuous variables using a 2D contour:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








Note that sometimes you may need to expand the axes a little bit to better show the contours:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12.5, NA)) + # NA means "don't change"
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))










Time Series
Since there isn’t really any time series data in the penguins dataset, we’ll take a quick detour and use the built-in economics dataset to explore visualizing a time series. In this case, we are looking at unemployment over time:

ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








geom_path() lets you explore how two variables are related over time. For example, unemployment and personal savings rate:

ggplot(economics, aes(x = unemploy / pop, y = psavert)) +
  geom_path(aes(colour = as.numeric(date))) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














NoteMultiple columns for individual aesthetics



Note how we’ve used multiple columns of the data to define the x-axis here. You can use any sort of mathematical operators to combine multiple columns into a single aesthetic, as long as you are doing row-wise math.





Combining layers
We can also combine multiple layers to show the same data in different ways in the same plot. For example, we could show the raw data for the above contour plot in addition to the contours:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(30, 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12, 23)) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) + # don't expand the axes so the background is all filled
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














NoteLayer order



When combining layers, the layers are added to the plot in order, so in this case the points are the bottom layer and the contour lines are the top layer. We changed the alpha of the middle layer to prevent the points from being blocked. I’ve also used the coord_cartesian() function to remove the default axis expansion. This way the background color reaches both axes and doesn’t have a white gap.




Facetting
Let’s take our scatterplot example from earlier:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








Now, what if we wanted to also split the data by the species of the penguins? We’re already using color and shape, so what other aesthetic could we use? We could possible use some shapes that have both a fill and outline color, but that sounds messy. Instead of using another aesthetic, we could also use a facet. This splits the chart into multiple panels:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  facet_wrap(vars(species), ncol = 1) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








We can get even crazier by faceting by multiple variables:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(species), cols = vars(year)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








OK, maybe we’ve gone a little too far here, but you get the picture!

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Combining plots
When publishing results, often we need to combine multiple figures into a single visualization. There are lots of packages for accomplishing this (even my own deeptime package has some functionality for it), but today we’ll check out the patchwork package which extends the “grammar of graphics” to combining plots (you may need to install it if you haven’t done so already).

library(patchwork)

First, let’s go ahead and make some plots. Instead of plotting them, though, we’ll save them as objects in our environment. Note that when you save a plot to an object it isn’t displayed in the “Plots” tab.

g1 <- ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

g2 <- ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(30, 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12, 23)) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

Now, in order to combine these, all we need to do is combine them using the + operator, like we did with the individual elements of the plots.

g1 + g2








You can see that patchwork does all of the work for us, lining up the different components of the plots. If we have more plots to combine, we can then use the | (side-by-side) and / (above-and-below) operators to make more complex arrangements of plots.

g3 <- ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

(g1 | g2) / g3








There’s a lot more you can do with patchwork, including adjusting the widths and heights and adding annotations and styling, but we’ll stop here for now.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Saving plots
The last big thing you’ll need to know about plotting is how to save your plots. ggplot2 comes with a nifty ggsave() function which you can use to save your plots in a number of different formats. Here we’ll save our most recent combined plot as both a PDF and a JPEG. The former is a vector format, meaning all of the elements of the figure as geometric shapes, and, because of this, none of the data is lost (aka “lossless”). The latter is a raster format, meaning the figure is converted to a 2-D array of colored pixels of a desired size, and because of this, some of the data is lost in the process (aka “lossy”). This results in the pixellation that you see when you zoom in on a JPEG. ggsave() detects what format you want based on the file extension, so we just need to specify the file location and the object to be saved (and optionally the dimensions of the output file). It’s usually a good idea to keep all figures in their own folder (which was already created for you).

gg <- (g1 | g2) / g3
ggsave("figures/penguins_1.pdf", gg, height = 10, width = 10)
ggsave("figures/penguins_1.jpg", gg, height = 10, width = 10)

Introduction
While you can make plots with just the packages that come bundled with base R, many R users make their visualizations entirely using the ggplot2 package and an ecosystem of packages designed around it.

# load the ggplot2 package
library(ggplot2)

To demonstrate this, we’ll be using the Palmer penguins dataset (built-in to R as of version 4.5.0). First, let’s load the dataset. Then let’s inspect the data using the glimpse() function.

data(penguins)
dplyr::glimpse(penguins)

Rows: 344
Columns: 8
$ species     <fct> Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Ad…
$ island      <fct> Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Tor…
$ bill_len    <dbl> 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, NA, 36.7, 39.3, 38.9, 39.2, 34.1, 42.0, …
$ bill_dep    <dbl> 18.7, 17.4, 18.0, NA, 19.3, 20.6, 17.8, 19.6, 18.1, 20.2, …
$ flipper_len <int> 181, 186, 195, NA, 193, 190, 181, 195, 193, 190, 186, 180,…
$ body_mass   <int> 3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250, …
$ sex         <fct> male, female, female, NA, female, male, female, male, NA, …
$ year        <int> 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007…


This dataset includes many different measurements for individual penguins from three different studies. The studies cover both sexes of three different species of penguins from three different islands in the Palmer Archipelago.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
The ggplot2 basics
The most important function in the ggplot2 package is ggplot(). Note that this function doesn’t include the “2” of the package name. Let’s go ahead and try using this function on our penguins data.

ggplot(penguins)








You’ll notice that the ggplot() function doesn’t actually do much by itself. Here, we provide it with the penguins dataset, but the result looks like someone started making a plot and then stopped after the first step of making the rectangle for the plot area. This is because ggplot2 is designed around the “grammar of graphics”. Therefore, it expects you to build a sentence-like structure out of its functions. A single word (i.e., the call to ggplot() above) doesn’t make much of a sentence, so let’s start building up a real sentence.
By using the ggplot() function, we are essentially stating that we are beginning a plotting “sentence”. We then combine this with other “words” (function calls) using the + operator. The next component you usually want to specify in a ggplot “sentence” is our “aesthetic” mappings. These specify the columns of the dataset that correspond to each axis of the plot, including the x/y axes, but also the axes of color, shape, etc. We do this with the aes() function:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len)








Hey, it’s starting to look like a plot now! Except there isn’t any actual data being plotted. Let’s fix that. We’ll start off with a simple scatter plot by using the geom_point() function:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len) +
  geom_point()








And there we go! You’ll notice that with just a few lines, we’ve already made a pretty nice visualization of this penguin data. ggplot2 does most of the work for us once we specify our dataset and our x and y variables.






NoteMissing data



You may have noticed a warning that some rows of the dataset contain missing values. There are two penguins without any measurements in the dataset. How might we remove them using dplyr so we don’t get this warning over and over?






CautionSolution






penguins <- penguins |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(body_mass))






Now, let’s go a step further and color the points by another variable (e.g., the island of the penguins). With ggplot2, all that requires is specifying another aesthetic:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island) +
  geom_point()








Notice that ggplot2 comes with its own default color scheme. However, I would strongly discourage you from using the default colors, especially as the number of categories increases (with only 3 categories here it isn’t too bad). Let’s try out some of the more accessible color palettes that are also available in R.
First, let’s try one of the viridis color palettes. Since this palette is included in ggplot2, all we need to do is add the proper “scale” to our ggplot() call. Scales tell ggplot how to handle a particular aesthetic, and are usually of the form scale_[aesthetic]_[type]().

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) # avoid yellow at the end of the palette








Now let’s try one of the brewer color palettes.

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")








Outside of color, there are many other aspects of the graph that we can modify using aesthetics and “scale”s. For example, we can modify the shape of the points:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")














NoteMore missing data



Urgh, more missing data! It appears that nine of the penguins are missing sex identification data. We can ignore the warning message, but that extra “NA” category in the legend is quite annoying. We can remove this category from the legend using na.translate = FALSE within scale_shape_discrete() (you could also use scale_shape_manual() if you wanted to supply your own shapes):

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE)










And the x/y axes:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)")

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Theming
The last basic thing you might want to do with ggplot2 is modify the style of the visualization. This is extremely customizable, but the first place to start is with a built-in theme. I personally prefer the classic theme, which looks very similar to base R plots:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic()








Using this built-in theme has changed many visual aspects of the graph, including changing the plot background color, adding axis lines, and removing the internal grid lines. If you look very closely, however, the axis tick labels are still a slight grey. We can use the theme() function to further customize the appearance and change this. In this case, we’ll make the axis text elements have a black color instead of the default gray.

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








And there we have it! With just 10 lines we’ve created what I would say is a publication quality graph! ggplot does a lot of the tedious work for us, giving us time to focus on the more important aspects, such as labeling and color. Admittedly, I’ve spent a LOT of time on these aspects in the past…
More information about all of the hierarchical theme components that you can customize is available here. In order to change many of these components, you need to use theme elements like we did above with element_text(). That and other theme elements are documented here.
