More complex features

Other layers
There are many other types of plots that we can make with ggplot2.

Histograms
We can visualize the density of values for a single variable with a histogram:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, fill = species) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














Note



Histograms don’t require a y-axis aesthetic by default. The counts are tabulated for you. If you specify a “fill” aesthetic, the default is to stack the bars which can sometimes be a bit misleading. You can also dodge them to fix this:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, fill = species) +
  geom_histogram(position = "dodge") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))












Boxplots and Violin Plotss
We can visualize the density of values for a single variable across a discrete variable with boxplots or violin plots:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))









ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_violin(scale = "width", draw_quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














NoteGeom options



Note that many of these “geom”s have lots of options. For example, here we’ve decided to scale all of the violin plots to the same width and to draw the quartiles on them (mimicking the boxplots above). You can see all of the options for a geom by checking out it’s help page (?geom_violin) or on the ggplot website.




2D Contours
We can also visualize the density of values across two continuous variables using a 2D contour:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








Note that sometimes you may need to expand the axes a little bit to better show the contours:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12.5, NA)) + # NA means "don't change"
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))










Time Series
Since there isn’t really any time series data in the penguins dataset, we’ll take a quick detour and use the built-in economics dataset to explore visualizing a time series. In this case, we are looking at unemployment over time:

ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








geom_path() lets you explore how two variables are related over time. For example, unemployment and personal savings rate:

ggplot(economics, aes(x = unemploy / pop, y = psavert)) +
  geom_path(aes(colour = as.numeric(date))) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














NoteMultiple columns for individual aesthetics



Note how we’ve used multiple columns of the data to define the x-axis here. You can use any sort of mathematical operators to combine multiple columns into a single aesthetic, as long as you are doing row-wise math.





Combining layers
We can also combine multiple layers to show the same data in different ways in the same plot. For example, we could show the raw data for the above contour plot in addition to the contours:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(30, 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12, 23)) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) + # don't expand the axes so the background is all filled
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














NoteLayer order



When combining layers, the layers are added to the plot in order, so in this case the points are the bottom layer and the contour lines are the top layer. We changed the alpha of the middle layer to prevent the points from being blocked. I’ve also used the coord_cartesian() function to remove the default axis expansion. This way the background color reaches both axes and doesn’t have a white gap.




Facetting
Let’s take our scatterplot example from earlier:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








Now, what if we wanted to also split the data by the species of the penguins? We’re already using color and shape, so what other aesthetic could we use? We could possible use some shapes that have both a fill and outline color, but that sounds messy. Instead of using another aesthetic, we could also use a facet. This splits the chart into multiple panels:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  facet_wrap(vars(species), ncol = 1) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








We can get even crazier by faceting by multiple variables:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(species), cols = vars(year)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








OK, maybe we’ve gone a little too far here, but you get the picture!

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Combining plots
When publishing results, often we need to combine multiple figures into a single visualization. There are lots of packages for accomplishing this (even my own deeptime package has some functionality for it), but today we’ll check out the patchwork package which extends the “grammar of graphics” to combining plots (you may need to install it if you haven’t done so already).

library(patchwork)

First, let’s go ahead and make some plots. Instead of plotting them, though, we’ll save them as objects in our environment. Note that when you save a plot to an object it isn’t displayed in the “Plots” tab.

g1 <- ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

g2 <- ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(30, 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12, 23)) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

Now, in order to combine these, all we need to do is combine them using the + operator, like we did with the individual elements of the plots.

g1 + g2








You can see that patchwork does all of the work for us, lining up the different components of the plots. If we have more plots to combine, we can then use the | (side-by-side) and / (above-and-below) operators to make more complex arrangements of plots.

g3 <- ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

(g1 | g2) / g3








There’s a lot more you can do with patchwork, including adjusting the widths and heights and adding annotations and styling, but we’ll stop here for now.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Saving plots
The last big thing you’ll need to know about plotting is how to save your plots. ggplot2 comes with a nifty ggsave() function which you can use to save your plots in a number of different formats. Here we’ll save our most recent combined plot as both a PDF and a JPEG. The former is a vector format, meaning all of the elements of the figure as geometric shapes, and, because of this, none of the data is lost (aka “lossless”). The latter is a raster format, meaning the figure is converted to a 2-D array of colored pixels of a desired size, and because of this, some of the data is lost in the process (aka “lossy”). This results in the pixellation that you see when you zoom in on a JPEG. ggsave() detects what format you want based on the file extension, so we just need to specify the file location and the object to be saved (and optionally the dimensions of the output file). It’s usually a good idea to keep all figures in their own folder (which was already created for you).

gg <- (g1 | g2) / g3
ggsave("figures/penguins_1.pdf", gg, height = 10, width = 10)
ggsave("figures/penguins_1.jpg", gg, height = 10, width = 10)

title: Share a package
text:
View source file
Having a package is nice but it’s much less useful if you keep it for you. There are two main, non-exclusive ways to share your package to the world:

title: Share a package
text:
Publish your package

Version control system
In this section, we assume you are already familiar with Git and GitHub. If this is not the case, then you might be interested in our module on these tools: <link>.
Supposing we put our package my.pkg on GitHub, R users can now install it with the following alternatives:
remotes::install_github("<username>/my.pkg")
pak::pak("<username>/my.pkg")






NoteCan I install packages from other platforms?



GitHub is the most famous platform to use Git features and store code. However, you could also use other platforms, such as Gitlab, Codeberg, or Forgejo.
Using these platforms will not affect the ability to install your package. For instance, if your host your package on Codeberg, then it can be installed with:
remotes::install_git("https://codeberg.org/<username>/my.pkg.git")
pak::pak("git::https://codeberg.org/<username>/my.pkg.git")




CRAN
CRAN is the Comprehensive R Archive Network. It is a general repository where packages can be stored, and it is where packages are installed from by default. Currently, there are more than 25,000 packages on CRAN (you can see the entire list here).
Puting a package on CRAN has several advantages. First, it gives your package more visibility, and it guarantees that it is easy to install it on almost all operating systems. Second, your package is constantly tested against new versions of R or with new versions of its dependencies. This guarantees that your package is compatible with the rest of the ecosystem at a given time.
This last point comes at a cost, however. If your test suite starts failing because of changes in R or in some of its dependencies, it becomes at risk of removal from CRAN. Usually, the CRAN team gives the package maintainer two or three weeks to fix the errors and submit a new version (although an extension can be requested if needed). Therefore, putting your package on CRAN doesn’t guarantee it will stay there and it requires you to be available for maintenance if needed.
Publishing a package on CRAN also means complying with a set of strict rules in terms of formatting or testing. This may sound intimidating but there exist many resources to make this process easier. For instance, there are a lot of packages to make your life easier (urlchecker to check invalid URLs, spelling to detect spelling mistakes, among others). There are also collaborative todo lists before submitting to CRAN, such as this one. Finally, the function devtools::release() provides a long checklist to ensure that your package is ready to be submitted.
We recommend reading this section of the “R packages” book for a list of good practices and things to do. This looks intimidating and it can be a non-negligible amount of work, but it becomes easier as you get more familiar with the package development process.

title: Share a package
text:
Make a package website
Publishing a package on GitHub or on CRAN makes it easy to install but not necessarily easy to discover. We can add something more: a website!
This might sound like a lot of work, but we are going to use a great package to build a package website in a few minutes: pkgdown.

Local website
We can create the website locally with pkgdown::build_site(). This takes care of everything:

converting documentation
create links to the Github repository
create pages for license, authors, etc.

This will automatically open a preview. Note that pkgdown uses all the information stored in DESCRIPTION, so you should ensure this is up to date!


Publish the website
The website can then be published via GitHub Pages, using a continuous integration workflow. To learn more about this, see the GitHub Actions section.

View source file
In this section, we will see how to create the basic structure of an R package, using a couple of functions created for the occasion.

title: Create a package
text:
Structure of a package
At a minimum, a package must have two folders:

R: contains all the .R files where we will write our functions
man: short for “manual”. This will contain all the documentation that is accessible with ? in R (for example ?factor)

While not mandatory, it is also recommended to have the following folders:

tests: contains all the tests for your package
vignettes: additional documentation that contains more extensive examples and tutorials for your package.

This section focuses on R and man, we will see how to populate these other folders in separate sections.

title: Create a package
text:
Practical example
The easiest way to learn how to make a package is to actually make one.
Let’s say that we have already two functions and that we use them in our work, but now we want to package them so that they are easier to share with coworkers. Our two functions are:

A function to compute the logarithm that returns NULL if the input is not numeric:


safe_log <- function(x) {
  if (is.numeric(x)) {
    log(x)
  } else {
    warning("Can't compute the logarithm of a non-numeric input.")
    NULL
  }
}
log("a")

Error in `log()`:
! non-numeric argument to mathematical function

safe_log("a")

Warning in safe_log("a"): Can't compute the logarithm of a non-numeric input.


NULL



A function to count the number of unique elements in a vector:


n_unique <- function(x) {
  length(unique(x))
}
n_unique(1:10)

[1] 10

n_unique(c(1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4))

[1] 4



Create the package
Let’s create a package called my.pkg. We can do this in various ways:

we can use usethis in an R console:

usethis::create_package("<path>/my.pkg")

with RStudio: File > New Project > New Directory > R Package > Name it, and choose its location

If we choose to do this with usethis, then we should see this:
✔ Creating my.pkg/.
✔ Setting active project to "/home/etienne/Desktop/Git/modules/my.pkg".
✔ Creating R/.
✔ Writing DESCRIPTION.
Package: my.pkg
Title: What the Package Does (One Line, Title Case)
Version: 0.0.0.9000
Authors@R (parsed):
    * First Last <first.last@example.com> [aut, cre]

License: `use_mit_license()`, `use_gpl3_license()` or friends to
    pick a license
Config/roxygen2/version: 8.1.0
Encoding: UTF-8
Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE)
✔ Writing NAMESPACE.
✔ Writing my.pkg.Rproj.

✔ Adding "^\\.Rproj\\.user$" to .Rbuildignore.
✔ Opening /home/etienne/Desktop/Git/modules/my.pkg/ in a new session.
✔ Setting active project to "<no active project>".
There is a lot of information to unpack here! We can see that this command created a folder my.pkg, an R folder inside it, and then it created multiple files: DESCRIPTION and NAMESPACE.
Printing the structure of the my.pkg folder may be useful here:
my.pkg
├── DESCRIPTION
├── NAMESPACE
├── R
└── my.pkg.Rproj






TipHow to print a tree structure as above?





If you have the package fs installed, you can use fs::dir_tree() with the path you want.
For example, if my.pkg is your working directory then you can simply call fs::dir_tree(), but if it is a subfolder then you need to call fs::dir_tree("my.pkg").



The DESCRIPTION file contains all the important information about our package:

who built it?
when?
what is the goal of the package?
what is the version of the package?
what are its dependencies?

and a lot more information.
The NAMESPACE file contains all the information about the functions that are imported and exported by our package. Imported functions are provided by other packages, meaning that these packages are now our dependencies. Exported functions are what our package provides, i.e. the functions made available to users of our packages after they call library(my.pkg) or when they use my.pkg::.
The R folder is where we are going to store our functions.


Add our functions
Let’s create two files in the R folder: n_unique.R and safe_log.R. We don’t need to create one file per function, we could just bundle everything in a single file. However, it is generally good practice to keep those separated, especially when we start creating more exported functions. We can now move the functions we created to each of these files:


R/n_unique.R

n_unique <- function(x) {
  length(unique(x))
}



R/safe_log.R

safe_log <- function(x) {
  if (is.numeric(x)) {
    log(x)
  } else {
    warning("Can't compute the logarithm of a non-numeric input.")
    NULL
  }
}

Our package structure now is:
my.pkg
├── DESCRIPTION
├── NAMESPACE
├── R
│   ├── n_unique.R
│   └── safe_log.R
└── my.pkg.Rproj
When we create a standalone function in a non-package project, we need to evaluate it in the R console to then be able to run it. Doing this for all functions in an R package would be very tedious. Moreover, the order in which R files are evaluated may matter. Therefore, we can use devtools::load_all() whenever we want to load the package we are currently developing:
> devtools::load_all()
ℹ Loading my.pkg
We are now be able to run our functions in the console! We have now populated one of the two mandatory folders (R), so let’s move on to the documentation process, which will lead to the creation of the man folder.

title: Create a package
text:
Document a function
The documentation of a function is done in the .R file: it will then automatically be converted to an .Rd file placed in the man folder. There is no need to create an .Rd file yourself!
Writing the documentation is similar to writing comments, but you need to use #' (with an apostrophe) instead of #.


R/n_unique.R

#' Title
#'
#' @description
#' Some description.
#'
#' @param x An input
#'
#' @return A numeric value indicating the number of unique values in the input.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' n_unique(c(1, 2, 1))

n_unique <- function(x) {
  length(unique(x))
}

Let’s go through these changes:

@description contains the text that appears between the title and the “Usage” section in a function help page. Usually it contains a few sentences describing the general purpose of the function.
@param is the description of the expected input (there can be several @param tags);
@return is the description of what this function returns;
@export indicates that this function is exported, i.e is available to users of this package;
@examples gives some examples that show how the function works.

These are roxygen2 tags, and there are many more that you can find here: https://roxygen2.r-lib.org/articles/rd.html.
Let’s now run devtools::document() to create the .Rd file.






NoteI have a ‘Skipping NAMESPACE’ message





Maybe devtools::document() will print the following message:
ℹ Updating my.pkg documentation
ℹ Loading my.pkg
✖ Skipping NAMESPACE
ℹ It already exists and was not generated by roxygen2.
In this case, delete NAMESPACE and run devtools::document() again.



You should see the following message:
ℹ Updating my.pkg documentation
ℹ Loading my.pkg
Writing n_unique.Rd
You should then be able to access the documentation of our function with ?n_unique.



We have the minimal documentation but you can make it much bigger. Note that we can also use Markdown syntax in the text.






CautionExercise



Your turn! Improve the documentation:

write a longer description for n_unique()
create the documentation for safe_log()
add more explanations in the @details section of safe_log()

Don’t forget to re-document so that your changes appear in .Rd files in man.


The help page is one of the first things users will check to learn about your functions. Give details and examples!
We now have the most basic structure of a working R package. Let’s build it!

title: Package development
text:
View source file






NoneLearning Objectives



After this module, you will:

Be able to convert standalone R functions to an R package
Know how to document, test, and share your package
Know how to set up continuous integration workflows to regularly test your package



An R package is a way to convert a collection of functions into a well-organised, documented, and ideally well-tested piece of software that other people can easily install and use. A lot of the work goes into the creation of functions (for which we have a module!).
This module will show you the multiple steps of R package development, from having a single standalone function, to creating, documenting, testing, and sharing a package.
It is easy to expand on many of these aspects, and we will cover the most important ones, but entire books are written on package development (and on software development in general). Therefore, we will purposely skip or not explore in depth some aspects of package development. This module is inspired by the “R Packages” book, and we recommend exploring this book more if you want to dig deeper on the topic on general, or on specific aspects only.
This module is divided in five parts:

Create a package: how to create the minimal structure of an R package
Test a package: how to build a test suite.
Develop a package: some good practices and considerations to keep in mind when developing an R package
Share a package: how to make your package installable by anyone
Use continuous integration: how to use GitHub or other platforms to check your package on every change

Before we start, we recommend installing these three packages:

View source file
We now know the basics of a package: how to create one, document it, and test it. But there are plenty of choices to make when developing a package, such as:
In this section, we are going to cover some of these questions and define some good practices when developing a package.

title: Develop a package
text:
Namespace

Namespace conflicts
As seen in the first section, the NAMESPACE file contains the list of functions that your package exports. When someone loads your package with library(my.pkg), all exported functions will be imported in the environment.
In the likely scenario where this user loads several packages, there can be a namespace conflict if two packages (or more) provide two functions with the same name. It is also possible that some of your functions have the same name as functions included by default in R. For example, dplyr overwrites several functions:
library(dplyr)

## Attaching package: ‘dplyr’
##
## The following object are masked from ‘package:stats’:
##  
##  filter, lag
##
## The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’:
##   
##  intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
While some tools are available on the user’s side to fix such conflicts (e.g see the package conflicted), it is good practice to try to avoid them. In particular, you should be very careful that your functions don’t have the same names as other functions in popular packages (e.g data.table, tidyverse packages, etc.).






TipHow do I know if a function name is already used?





The package pkgcheck allows us to quickly check whether a function name is already provided by a package on CRAN. For instance, filter() is exported by multiple packages:

pkgcheck::fn_names_on_cran("filter")

         package version fn_name
1  cohortBuilder   1.0.0  filter
2         crunch  1.31.3  filter
3          dplyr   1.2.1  filter
4        gsignal   0.3-7  filter
5         narray   0.5.2  filter
6      pammtools   0.8.1  filter
7  pandocfilters   0.1-6  filter
8           rTLS 0.2.6.1  filter
9            rbi   1.0.1  filter
10        signal   1.8-1  filter
11        tidyft  0.9.20  filter
12       tidylog   1.1.0  filter
13     tidytable  0.11.2  filter
14   rjd3filters   2.4.0  filter
15        vectra  0.14.1  filter
16       poorman   0.3.0  filter







S3 methods
In certain cases, we can address namespace conflicts by using S3 methods. This is the mechanism that allows R users to call summary() or plot() on a lot of different objects while not having namespace conflicts.
A function like summary() is called an S3 generic. When we first call this function, it gets dispatched to one of the existing S3 methods based on the class of the first input (in this case, object). For instance, let’s make a linear regression and store its output in res:

res <- lm(mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars)
class(res)

[1] "lm"


As we can see, res is an object of class "lm". When I call summary(res), summary() will see that class and look for the method summary.lm() (more generally, it will look for the method summary.<class>()). In this case, summary.lm is implemented in base R:
> summary.lm
function (object, correlation = FALSE, symbolic.cor = FALSE, 
    ...) 
{
    [truncated by hand]
}
<bytecode: 0x599a48d052d0>
<environment: namespace:stats>
Packages can also provide their own methods for existing generics! For instance, in our package, we could have our functions return objects of class "my.class" and define a custom summary.my.class() so that we could simply call summary() on our objects.






TipVisualising S3 dispatch





The package sloop allows us to see how S3 dispatch works:

sloop::s3_dispatch(summary(res))

=> summary.lm
 * summary.default


In this case, our call to summary(res) found two relevant methods: summary.lm() is the one that is called, and summary.default() is the one that would have been used as fallback if there were no summary.lm().



Implementing methods for well-known generics such as summary(), plot(), mean(), quantile(), and many others, is a good way to reduce namespace conflicts while ensuring a good user experience.






NoteHow do I know which functions are generic?



You can check whether a function is generic by printing it in the console, as it will call UseMethod() internally:
> quantile
function (x, ...) 
UseMethod("quantile")
<bytecode: 0x599a488ea330>
<environment: namespace:stats>
Another way to know this is to use sloop::is_s3_generic():
> sloop::is_s3_generic("quantile")
[1] TRUE

title: Develop a package
text:
Dependencies

To take or not to take dependencies



When we develop a package, we can import other packages, either because they provide essential features or simply because they make the development process easier. These packages are now dependencies of our package, meaning that our package can be affected if any of these packages has some issues.
The topic of dependencies is very important in software in general, not just in R packages. Taking dependencies is a tradeoff.
On one hand, we can rely on the work and experience of others to use features that would be hard and/or time-consuming to implement ourselves. Splitting functionalities across packages can also be a good thing since each package can focus on some particular aspects instead of being a collection of hundreds of functions that is harder to properly document and test. It is also important to keep in mind that not all dependencies are equal. Depending on a small package that does one thing very well and that is actively maintained is often better than reinventing the wheel (maybe with a worse implementation) in our package.
On the other hand, dependencies can make our package more fragile because changes in these dependencies also affect your package. For example, if a package that we depend on changes their function and argument names, then we need to update our package to take this into account, otherwise our code would break. This kind of changes is called breaking changes.
There are more aspects to consider when deciding whether to depend on other packages, and these are nicely summarised in this blog post.
This might seem a bit abstract, so let’s see a concrete example.






NoteAbout software security





Whether to use external dependencies can be particularly important in terms of software security, but this is not our focus here. If you want to learn more about this topic, search for software supply chain.





An example
Suppose that for some reason, our package uses the function select_vars() from the package dplyr. This function was removed in dplyr v.1.1.0, which has implications for users of our package:

if their version of dplyr is < 1.1.0, it still works fine;
if their version of dplyr is >= 1.1.0, then the function in your package that uses select_vars() will error.

In this case, we could replace select_vars() by another function and indicate that the version of dplyr must be greater than or equal to 1.1.0, so that users would at least know why this function fails if they don’t have a supported version.
Having dependencies forces us to stay aware of changes in these dependencies, and this increases the maintenance burden.


How to use dependencies
Information on dependencies is kept in DESCRIPTION. We can list dependencies in two fields: Imports or Suggests.
Adding a package in Imports signals that it has to be present on the user’s machine for our package to work. Therefore, this dependency will be installed whenever a user installs our package.
Adding a package in Suggests signals that some functionalities of our package require this dependency but it is not essential. For instance, testthat could be listed here because it is required for testing but not having it installed doesn’t change anything for the end user of our package. Dependencies listed in Suggests will not be installed automatically when a user installs our package.
We can either add a dependency by hand, or use usethis::use_package() to add it automatically. For example, if we choose to put dplyr and sf in Imports, and testthat in Suggests, then our DESCRIPTION file will look like this:
[ manually truncated ]
Imports: 
    dplyr,
    sf
Suggests: 
    testthat (>= 3.0.0)
As you can see, we can also specify minimum version requirements for our dependencies. Going back to our example with dplyr above, in addition to making the necessary fixes to handle breaking changes in dplyr 1.1.0, we should specify that dplyr (>= 1.1.0) is required in our package.
There are several ways to use dependencies in our code:

using ::, for instance dplyr::select();
importing a specific function by putting #' @importFrom dplyr select in the function documentation and then calling devtools::document(). This will add importFrom(dplyr, select) in NAMESPACE, meaning that we can use select() directly in our code.

Note that if a package is in Suggests, then we need to check whether it is installed before calling it in our code. For instance, if our function depends on a function from the package foo, we can check its presence with:
my_fun <- function(a, b) {
  if (!requireNamespace("foo", quietly = TRUE)) {
    stop(
      "Package \"foo\" must be installed to use this function.",
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }
  # code that includes calls such as foo::some_function()
}


Reverse dependencies
So far, our focus was on dependencies, i.e. packages that we depend on. If our package becomes useful enough, then maybe other developers will choose to depend on it. Packages that depend on our package are called “reverse dependencies”.
This means that any change we make to our package might affect other packages. It is good practice to check these reverse dependencies before releasing a new version of our package:

if we don’t find any new failure in these reverse dependencies, then we know that our new version won’t break them;
if we find new failures then we should notify the maintainers of these dependencies. If the failures are not too big, we can also submit a patch ourselves, but this is not mandatory. In general, we should give these maintainers a couple of weeks notice before releasing our new version.

We can use the package revdepcheck to run reverse dependency checks.






NoteHow do reverse dependency checks work?





When we check reverse dependencies, we want to ensure that our changes do not cause new failures. A reverse dependency might already have failing tests which are not related to our changes.
Tools to check reverse dependencies will install the latest version of our package and its development version (where we made new changes) and run the test suite of each reverse dependency with both versions. A failure happening only when the development version of our package is used means that our changes cause reverse dependency failures.



Note that if we eventually publish our package on CRAN (cf. next section), then the CRAN team will automatically run reverse dependency checks when we submit a new version. Failures in reverse dependencies will only be tolerated if we have notified maintainers in advance.

title: Contribute to our packages
text: This page details the process to contribute code or documentation to one of our R packages. See the general guide to learn more ways to contribute to Palaeoverse.

title: Contribute to our packages
text:
Required tools
Besides R, you will need to use a variety of tools to ease the development process and to ensure that your contribution follows the Palaeoverse code standards.

R packages:

devtools: this contains many functions that make package development significantly easier

pak: this provides some functions to install all dependencies of the package you want to contribute to. It is good to install optional dependencies because some tests or examples will use them.

Other tools (see screenshots below):

Air: this is a code formatter, it ensures that all R code in the package follows a common style (e.g. it automatically adds whitespace or breaks lines where needed). You can install it from here: https://posit-dev.github.io/air/cli.html
You might need to restart RStudio (or the IDE that you use, if you use one) after installing it. This tool runs in the terminal, not the R console. You can check that it is correctly installed by running air -V to print its version number.
Jarl: this is a code linter, it checks R code to find common mistakes or programming patterns that shouldn’t be used because they are less readable, efficient, or prone to bugs. You can install it from here: https://jarl.etiennebacher.com/#installation
You might need to restart RStudio (or the IDE that you use, if you use one) after installing it. This tool runs in the terminal, not the R console. You can check that it is correctly installed by running jarl -V to print its version number.






Git: this is a version control tool, which is key in the software development process. It allows us to make and suggest changes to packages.
Github: this is the platform that stores the code for all of Palaeoverse. It also provides the interface to suggest, review, and implement code changes. Create a Github account if you don’t have one already.

You can check some of our workshop materials to see how to get started with Git, Github, and RStudio. Alternatively, the book “Happy Git and Github for the useR” is a useful, and free, resource. In this tutorial, we assume that you have already done these steps.
The remainder of this guide requires you to be familiar with a few Git actions: cloning, committing, branching, and pushing.

title: Contribute to our packages
text:
Get ready to contribute
You need to have an idea of what you want to change in the package. This could be a typo to fix or a new function argument to implement, among other things. You can take a look at all issues in Palaeoverse for inspiration. Note that almost all pull requests should refer to an issue (except for those that fix typos in the documentation for instance). If you can’t find an existing issue that discusses the changes you want to make, create one and ensure that making a pull request (PR) is necessary before opening one.
Once you have installed the tools detailed above and know what you want to do, it is time to fork and clone the relevant repository so that you have a local copy you can modify. You can then create a new branch that very briefly summarizes the type of change, e.g. “fix-typo-palaeorotate” or “add-arg-XXX-lat-bins-degrees”. Giving a readable name to a branch makes it easier to switch between branches in the future. It is also important to create a new branch early in the process so that we avoid pushing to “main” by mistake.

Once this is done, run pak::local_install_dev_deps() to install all packages used by this package (e.g. because they provide some functionality that is essential to the package, or because they help in the development process but are not strictly necessary for external users).
Before we start: contributing to an R package requires touching several files and understanding many concepts. It is absolutely fine to open PRs that are still work-in-progress and to ask for help where you are stuck. We are not expecting complete PRs from everyone.
Now that you have all development tools installed and created a new branch, you are ready to code!

title: Contribute to our packages
text:
Case study: “Improved binning for time_bins”
In this section, we will use an existing merged pull request as a case study to see the various steps in the development process. More specifically, we will use PR #131 (“Improved binning for time_bins”) of the palaeoverse package. You can open this link and go to the tab “Files changed” if you want to follow along. Note, this is a legacy PR and the function has evolved since this PR, it is only meant as an illustration for the contributing process.
The PR that we follow (“Improved binning for time_bins”) is a new feature: it adds the argument n_bins to time_bins() and improves this function’s performance. If you check the “Files changed” tab on Github, you can see that four files were modified:

man/time_bins.Rd
R/time_bins.R

tests/testthat/test-time_bins.R
NEWS.md

We will explain these changes in more detail in the following subsections.

Implement changes
The first thing to do is to run devtools::load_all(). This will load the current version of the package in the session. This is extremely useful because it means that you can easily test changes you make: any time you change something in the code, run devtools::load_all() to load these changes and experiment with them. For now, we haven’t touched anything, so this simply loads the latest version of the package.
At this point, steps to follow start diverging depending on what you want to do. If you want to fix a bug, you should first ensure that you can reproduce the bug in the current version of the package, before changing anything.
Here, the PR we follow is a new feature so we don’t have to test anything before starting writing code. In this PR, the bulk of the work is done in R/time_bins.R: this file contains the implementation of palaeoverse::time_bins(), and is where the new argument is implemented and where the code is modified to improve the function’s performance. This tutorial gives an overview of the development process so we will not go through all of the code here, but instead just highlight the major steps.






NoteAbout R packages’ structure



R packages follow a strict structure and should at least have the following folders:

R: contains all the R code related to the functions provided by the package. The function documentation is usually stored in the same file as the code (this documentation consists of comments starting with #').
man: this is short for “manual”. It contains the final documentation exported by the package. This is the content that we see when we do ?mean for instance. Files in this folder are automatically generated by devtools::document(), you shouldn’t modify them by hand.
tests: contains the tests for all the functions in the package.

Therefore, a pull request that improves the efficiency of a function but doesn’t change anything from the user point of view will only modify files in the R folder. Conversely, adding a new function or a new argument requires changes in R, man, and tests.




Ensure package-level robustness
Unlike when writing code for a research project, code contained in an R package must be stress-tested to ensure that users can only run it in the intended way. A key part of this is input error handling: these are checks that ensure that the values passed to our function arguments are appropriate for the downstream code.
Here, a new argument has been added to the function (n_bins), so we need to add error handling on this argument, specifically to ensure that a value has been provided, and that it is numeric.
if (!is.numeric(n_bins) && !is.null(n_bins)) {  
  stop("`n_bins` should be a 'numeric' or NULL.")  
}  
Crafting robust error handling is difficult! Start by thinking about what characteristics are shared by a range of appropriate values, and what would exclude inappropriate values. You can look at how other functions check inputs and how existing tests cover a variety of wrong inputs for inspiration. Ultimately we will include the error handling in our review process, so we can help you to ensure that inappropriate values are caught.
Note: after this PR was merged, we added some helper functions to make input checking easier, e.g. rlang::check_bool(x) to ensure that x can only be TRUE or FALSE.


Document changes
Depending on the changes you have made, you might need to add documentation or modify existing ones. Function documentation uses roxygen2. This means that you can modify the documentation in the same R file where you made changes (here, R/time_bins.R) and then compile it to automatically produce ‘manual’ files in the man folder (here, man/time_bins.Rd). Function documentation starts with #' in the R file. For instance, we can see that the docs for the new argument were added here:
#' @param n_bins \code{numeric}. For equal-length time bins, a   
#'   fixed number of time bins can be specified instead of a bin  
#'   `size`. This argument will be ignored if `size` is specified.  
Once you have made the required changes, use devtools::document() to compile the documentation. This automatically generates man/time_bins.Rd, you don’t need to modify this file by hand!


Test changes
If your contribution consists of fixing a bug or implementing a new feature, then you must add tests, i.e. checks that assess whether a function works in the desired fashion. This is necessary to ensure that the bug will not go unnoticed again in the future, or that the feature behaves as you expect, especially when future modifications are made to the package.
Tests are implemented with the package testthat. This broadly consists of two sets of functions:

test_that(...) is the general block where you define the name of the test (i.e. what this block is supposed to test) and where you write the code to test and the expectations it is supposed to match;

expect_*() are functions that help define what should happen. There are many expectations possible, e.g. expect_equal() to test values, expect_length() to test the length of an object, and expect_true() to test that an assertion is true. See the full list here.

You can find existing tests in tests/testthat. If you modified an existing function, then find the corresponding test file (tip: usethis::use_test() will open the corresponding test file). If you created a function, you should create a new test file. Here, the PR we follow added an argument to time_bins() so we need to add some tests to the existing file tests/testthat/test-time_bins.R.
You can run devtools::test() at any point in the development process to run the entire test suite. This is also helpful for finding bugs in new code, as it automatically flags when the code is not behaving as it should.
In RStudio, you can also use the button “Test” in the “Build” pane:

A good place to start is to try and throw errors from any new argument input error handling (and if you get an unexpected result, it’s worth revisiting the error handling). Looking at files changed in this PR, we can see three types of changes:

This PR modified time_bins() to print a message when the number of bins is automatically determined, so this existing test:
expect_equal(
  nrow(time_bins(interval = c("Phanerozoic"),  size = 25, rank = "stage")),
  22
)  
is now wrapped in expect_message():
expect_message(  
  expect_equal(
    nrow(time_bins(interval = c("Phanerozoic"),  size = 25, rank = "stage")),
    22
  )  
)  
Tests for the new behavior when it is expected to work:
# check that size- and n_bins-based bins are identical  
expect_message({bins_n <- time_bins(n_bins = 11)})  
expect_message({bins_size <- time_bins(size = 50)})  
expect_equal(bins_n, bins_size)  
Tests for the new behavior when it is expected to fail:
expect_error(time_bins(n_bins = 200))  

Note: this PR is slightly outdated in terms of coding practices. In particular, you should now use expect_snapshot(<code>, error = TRUE) instead of expect_error(<code>).
Your pull request will not be merged until the code is adequately tested, with all tests passing. In general, we aim for at least 95% of code coverage for new functions. Note that an automated comment detailing the coverage of your PR and indicating which lines are not covered will be posted shortly after you open a PR (you can also use the package covr to check this locally).


All the rest
We have now added a feature, added multiple tests, ensured that the entire test suite succeeds, and potentially added some extra documentation. We are almost done! But there are a few things left to do before opening a new pull request.
First, we should communicate our changes to the users (unless the contribution consists of typo fixes). This is done via the NEWS.md file, which contains the list of all changes that are relevant to external users (sometimes we make changes that improve the package but are invisible to the external users because they don’t change any existing behavior). Depending on your change, add a bullet point in “New features” or “Bug fixes”.
Second, we should ensure that our changes match the Palaeoverse standards in terms of code quality and styling. To do so, we can use two automated tools, Air and Jarl. As mentioned in the “Required tools” section, the former automatically formats code, and the latter automatically searches for bad patterns of code. Run air format . and jarl check . in the terminal (not the R console). Air shouldn’t error but it may happen that Jarl reports some errors, in which case you will have to fix them. It might be the case that running jarl check . --fix automatically fixes those errors.
Finally, run devtools::check(). This is a thorough checking function that includes devtools::test() but also runs a lot of other checks.
If all checks pass, you are ready to create a PR!


Make a new pull request
Commit all your changes to your branch, and then push your branch. On the GitHub repository, you should now see a yellow block suggesting to “Compare and open a pull request”. You can follow this button to prepare a PR.

You will need to add a title and a PR description. Prepare a concise description that explains the new feature or the bug fix. Note that if this PR is related to an issue, you can add “Fixes #[ISSUE NUMBER]” or “Closes #1234” in the PR description (not the PR title) to automatically link the issue and PR, which will also close the issue 1234 when the PR is merged.
Once this is done, you can open the pull request. This triggers a list of automated checks to run tests, check formatting, etc. Some of these checks will post an automated comment in case of failure, explaining the issue and how to solve it. If this is not the case, you will need to open their logs and investigate why they fail (feel free to ask for help if you cannot figure out the cause of failure).


Handle reviewers’ comments
Opening a PR is a big step, but it rarely is the end of the contributing process. You have spent some time on this PR (sometimes a long time) but package maintainers haven’t, and they may have some comments and questions that you will need to address. In the case of our example PR, the conversation contained more than 30 comments between the author and the reviewers.
After spending a long time on a PR, having a lot of back and forth with package maintainers can feel frustrating, even adversarial at some point. The Tidyverse code review principle is a very good resource to understand the various aspects of code review and to learn more about the reviewers’ point of view. In short, the following points are essential:

Don’t take it personally

Never respond in anger to code review comments

Fix the code

Think collaboratively

We all have the same objective: having good quality packages. Once your PR meets all code standards, passes all checks, and you have addressed all comments, your PR will be merged.
Thank you, and congrats!

title: Zulip User Guide
text: Zulip is an organized, asynchronous team chat app (mobile and desktop) for distributed teams of all sizes. The application has many useful features that allow for the creation of easy-to-follow, well-organised conversations that will not disappear, and can be viewed/interacted with at any time by users around the world.

title: Zulip User Guide
text:
Zulip Structure & Interaction
Zulip organises conversations into channels (listed with a globe icon on the left-hand side of the app/webpage) (Fig. 1A). Each of these covers a broad theme. The Palaeoverse Public Workspace is formed from eight channels:

Events
Funding
Jobs
Publications
Resources
Community
Help
Announcements

As a guest user, you will be able to post in the first seven of these (all channels bar “Announcements”), and interact with all of them. These channels were established by Palaeoverse administrators, and will remain constant. Although you won’t personally be able to create a new channel, we will consider any requests, and you should contact the administrators if you wish to add something new.




Figure 1: Channels and topics in the Palaeoverse Zulip workspace.



Within each channel, conversations are organised into topics (Fig. 1B). This means that many discussions can happen simultaneously within the same channel, and everyone can respond in their own time without the feed becoming confusing. To view the existing topics, just click on the channel you are interested in. When you want to start up a new conversation or post about an opportunity, you should create a new topic as follows (Fig. 2):

Choose a relevant channel.
Click the “start a new topic” button (square with a plus symbol inside) located next to the channel name.
Enter the topic name (see below on how this should be formatted).
Compose your message relating to the topic in the text box. If you would like to, you can preview your message before it is sent using the eye symbol.
Click the “send” button (arrow shaped).





Figure 2: Composing topics and messages in the Palaeoverse Zulip workspace.



Once a topic is created, all users will be able to respond to this. When you start composing a response, it will automatically be addressed to the topic that you are reading or have clicked on. This will be confirmed in the textbox with the text: Message #Channel Name > Topic Name (Fig. 3). If your message is posted in the wrong place, it may be moved by administrators. Don’t worry if this happens, it is just to keep the space organised!




Figure 3: Responding to topics in the Palaeoverse Zulip workspace.

title: Zulip User Guide
text:
Topic templates
To keep channels easy to navigate, we have provided channel-specific templates that should aim to be used when starting a new topic. These are provided below.

Events
The Palaeoverse Zulip workspace welcomes event (e.g. conference and workshop) advertisements on the themes of palaeontology and open science, as well as other relevant themes such as ecology and conservation science.
Topics posted within the Events channel should aim to take the full name of the event being advertised, but shortened versions will be allowed if the title length exceeds 60 characters (Zulip-imposed limit).
The initial post within the topic thread should try to take the following format, or similar:

Event name (in bold):
Location:
Dates:
Additional Details (if applicable):
Link to the conference web page:

All other information (e.g. registration reminders, circular updates) and discussion relating to a specific conference or workshop should be posted below the relevant topic.


Publications
Relevant publications on the themes of phylogenetics, palaeobiogeography, palaeoecology, palaeoclimate, diversity dynamics, geometric morphometrics, statistical analyses, conservation, open science, etc., should be posted here.
Topics within the Publications channel should take the full title of the paper, but shortened versions will be allowed if the title length exceeds 60 characters.
The initial post within the topic should aim to take the following format, or similar:

APA-format citation (in bold):
DOI link:
Abstract/Additional Details:

All discussion relating to the research paper should be posted below the relevant topic.


Jobs
The Palaeoverse Zulip workspace welcomes relevant job advertisements in the fields of palaeontology, ecology, open science, conservation science, etc. Academic employment opportunities should include PhD positions, even if these are technically studentships.
Topics within the Jobs channel should aim to take the job title and hiring institution, but shortened versions will be allowed if the title length exceeds 60 characters.
The initial post within the topic should try to take the following format, or similar:

Job title (in bold):
Location:
Hours:
Salary:
Closing Date:
Additional Details:
Link to the job web page:

Any other information relating to a specific job should be posted below the relevant topic.


Funding
The Palaeoverse Zulip workspace welcomes all relevant funding advertisements. Grant opportunities are encouraged for all career stages, and can target both academic and non-academic audiences.
Topics within the Funding channel should aim to take the grant name and funding body being advertised, but shortened versions will be allowed if the title length exceeds 60 characters.
The initial post within the topic should try take the following format, or similar:

Grant title (in bold):
Awarding body:
Closing Date:
Additional Details:
Link to application page:

Any other information relating to the funding opportunity should be posted below the relevant topic.


Resources
The Resources channel is broad in its scope. Posts are welcomed on topics such as websites, books, talks, and course materials. As the breadth of subjects posted here cover a wider range, no specific post template is provided; however, the topic title should remain short and descriptive.
All discussion relating to the advertised resource should be posted in the relevant topic thread.


Community
The Community channel is also broad in its scope. This is a place to share things such as surveys, open nominations for awards, competitions, society news, or other community-focused topics. As the subjects posted here could be highly variable in nature, no specific post template is provided; however, the topic title should remain short and descriptive.
All discussion relating to the post should be written in the relevant topic thread.


Help
The Help channel can be used for questions relating to the topics of palaeontology, ecology, open science, conservation science, etc. As the breadth of subjects posted here will cover quite a wide range, no template is provided; however, the topic title should remain short and descriptive.
All responses to questions should be placed in the relevant topic thread.


Announcements
Posts within the Announcements channel will be used for announcements relating to the workspace, e.g. changes in operation, code of conduct, and wider user messages. These messages will only be permitted from members and administrators; however, as a user you will be able to interact with these.

When using the Palaeoverse Zulip Public Workspace, it is important to act in a way that is conducive to a positive and enriching environment. Credit/Attribution for Shared Work

Published work
When sharing work (e.g. published papers, artwork) the appropriate credit should always be provided in the same post if it is not immediately obvious who the work can be attributed to.
Example 1: a post with a link to a paper does not need to be accompanied by any additional text as all accreditations (e.g. authors and publisher) are made clear within the link.
Example 2: a post comprising a single illustration file should be accompanied by additional text to provide accreditation.


Unpublished work
Unpublished data should not be posted unless there is explicit approval from its creator/owner. It is important to remember that all posts in the public channels can be viewed by anybody with access to the internet.

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text: Palaeoverse was established in 2022 as a community-driven initiative dedicated to advancing open science through shared tools, training, and resources. To help ensure that our community remains inclusive and respectful, we feel that it is important to establish some expectations of behaviour when interacting within our spaces.

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text:
Scope
This Code of Conduct (CoC) applies to all individuals interacting in all Palaeoverse community spaces and activities, whether conducted in person or online. This includes, but is not limited to, GitHub repositories, Zulip channels, lecture series, workshops, meetings, and other community-sponsored events. In using these platforms, individuals confirm that they understand the CoC and consent to their behaviour being held against the standards defined in this document.
The CoC also applies to individuals when they are representing Palaeoverse or its community in public or professional contexts. Representation of the community may include, but is not limited to, the use of an official Palaeoverse email address, posting through an official social media account, or serving as a designated representative at online or in-person events.

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text:
Our Pledge
We as members, contributors, and leaders of Palaeoverse strive to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, irrespective of personal characteristics such as age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, religion, marital status, parental status, or sexual identity and orientation.
We promise to act and interact in ways that foster an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text:
Our Standards
Examples of behavior that contribute to a positive environment for our community include:

Demonstrating empathy and kindness towards other people

Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences

Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback

Accepting responsibility and apologising to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience

Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind

Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks

Public or private harassment

Publishing others’ private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission

Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text:
Enforcement
Any conduct that poses an immediate or significant threat to the safety of individuals or the public, or that may constitute a criminal offence, should be reported promptly to the appropriate law enforcement authorities.
Instances of other abusive, harassing, discriminatory, or otherwise unacceptable behavior that contradict the terms laid out in this CoC may be reported to Pedro Godoy and Bethany Allen via the “Report Misconduct” form linked at the bottom of the Code of Conduct Page on our website. Alternatively, if the breach of rules occurs during an in-person meeting and requires immediate action, the incident can be reported (either by email or in-person) to one of the physically-present Palaeoverse team members. Where possible, individuals making a report are encouraged to provide any information or supporting documentation that may assist in understanding and addressing the concerns raised.
Anonymous reporting is available through the “Report Misconduct” form; however, it should be understood that this form of complaint may limit the ability of those responsible for reviewing the report to seek clarification, request additional information, or provide updates regarding the outcome. Anonymous reports will nevertheless be considered and addressed to the greatest possible extent.
Individuals who do not feel comfortable using the reporting form may instead contact members of the Palaeoverse Core Team directly via email. Reports will be handled as confidentially as possible, consistent with the need to investigate concerns and protect the safety and well-being of community members. All members of the community who receive reports are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text:
Enforcement Procedure
All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly. Upon receiving the report, a meeting will be convened comprising at least three Palaeoverse Core Team members. If any Palaeoverse Core Team Member has a close professional or personal relationship with any of the parties involved, they should declare a conflict of interest and excuse themself from the meeting/decision making.
Meetings will aim to convene as soon as possible, and at least within 14 days of the complaint being received. If the complaint is made during an in-person event (e.g. workshop), the meeting should ideally occur on the same day as the report’s receival.
Once the Palaeoverse Core Team members present at the meeting have reviewed the complaint, they will determine whether any further information from the reporter and/or the reported party is required and will contact the appropriate party/parties to acquire this. Both parties should use this opportunity to provide any additional information they deem pertinent to the case. Once a decision has been reached, both the reporter and reported party (if previously contacted by Palaeoverse relating to the investigation) will receive written confirmation detailing any actions to be taken.
The reported party will be permitted to appeal the decision in the case of any new information coming to light. Once this information has been received, an additional meeting should be held by the Palaeoverse Core Team members, following the same timeline as laid out above for the initial report.
All Palaeoverse Core Team members retain the right and responsibility to immediately remove or reject written or spoken comments, posts, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned with this CoC without the need to convene a meeting. They will communicate reasons for their moderation decisions when appropriate. Consequences for the responsible party will be determined following a meeting of at least three Palaeoverse Core Team members. The party responsible for the breach of conduct will receive written confirmation detailing any consequences in line with our “Enforcement Responsibilities”.

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text:
Enforcement Responsibilities
Palaeoverse Core Team members are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will aim to take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.
The following guidelines will be used by Palaeoverse Core Team members in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

1. Correction
Offence: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.
Consequence: A private, written warning from the Palaeoverse Core Team will be issued, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. An apology to the impacted individuals may be requested.


2. Warning
Offence: A violation through a single incident, or a series of actions that have previously resulted in a correction.
Consequence: A formal warning will be issued, with additional consequences for any continued misconduct. The individual will be prohibited, for a specified period, from interacting with the people involved, including any unsolicited contact with those responsible for enforcing the Code of Conduct. This prohibition applies across all community spaces and external communication channels, including social media. Any violation of these restrictions may result in a temporary or permanent ban.


3. Temporary Ban
Offence: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior that has previously warranted corrections or warnings.
Consequence: A temporary ban will be imposed, prohibiting all participation, interaction, and public communication within the community. The duration of the ban will be determined on a case-by-case basis. During this period, the individual must not engage in any public or private contact with the people involved, including any unsolicited communication with those responsible for enforcing the Code of Conduct. Violation of these restrictions may result in a permanent ban.


4. Permanent Ban
Offence: An incident of gross misconduct, a pattern of violation of community standards (including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals), or breaking of a temporary ban.
Consequence: A permanent ban will be enforced, prohibiting all participation, engagement, and public interaction within the community.

title: AI Policy
text:
Palaeoverse is a community-driven initiative advancing open science in palaeontology through shared tools, training, and resources. Part of this initiative is to enable researchers at every career stage to learn and develop new technical and social skills. The human aspect of this work is therefore important to us and we are committed to maintaining spaces for human interaction and engagement. We acknowledge the potential usefulness and growing prevalence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), but wish to see it used only where reasonable and appropriate, whilst prioritising accuracy, accessibility, and upskilling.
The objective of this policy is to provide some guidelines regarding AI usage on our various platforms, such as Github and Zulip. This policy is adapted from Zulip’s AI policy.

title: AI Policy
text:
AI for communication
Do not post AI-generated messages: Zulip messages, Github issues, pull request (PR) descriptions, and other messages must be written by humans. If you need to quote an AI answer in a conversation, put the answer in a quote block (starting with “>” in Markdown) to distinguish AI output from your own thoughts.
You can use any tool you like for help with spelling, grammar, or translation, but ultimately must take personal responsibility for the messages you post.

title: AI Policy
text:
AI for coding
You can use any tool that helps you understand the Palaeoverse code repositories and write good code, including AI tools. If you used AI to generate code, you must disclose it in the pull request description and mention the tool and version used (e.g. Claude Opus 4.8, or OpenAI Codex 5.3). Additionally, you always need to understand and explain the changes you’re proposing to make, whether or not you used an AI as part of your process to produce them. The answer to “Why is X an improvement?” should never be “I’m not sure. The AI did it.”.
Do not submit an AI-generated PR you haven’t personally understood and tested.
Changes in documentation (e.g. documenting a new function argument, adding a vignette, editing the changelog) can be based on AI output, but it remains your responsibility to read through the entire text and ensure that it makes sense to you and represents your ideas concisely. It needs to be understood and appreciated by human readers. A good rule of thumb is that if you can’t make yourself carefully read some AI output that you generated, nobody else will want to read it either.

title: AI Policy
text:
Rule violations
Not following these rules will be treated as a Code of Conduct violation and will be addressed as detailed in the “Enforcement guidelines” section.
